The migration that lost the notes column still sits badly with me. Mara had asked for something small: split the customers table so that billing addresses lived in a table of their own. I wrote the script in an afternoon, we read it through together, and it looked tidy. What neither of us noticed was that my copy step selected the columns by name from a list I had typed out by hand, and the list did not include the free-text notes field that the support people had been filling in for four years. The new table was created, the old one was dropped, and four years of small human remarks, things like who prefers a phone call and whose invoices must go to a sister, were simply not carried over.

We found out nine days later, when Odile from support asked why every customer suddenly looked like a stranger. Mara went quiet in the way she does when something is truly wrong, and then she asked me, quite gently, whether the nightly dumps still went back that far. They went back seven days. Nine was two too many. In the end we recovered about two thirds from an export Odile had made for a spreadsheet in the spring, and the rest was gone for good.

What I took from it was not only the obvious rule about never listing columns by hand. It was that I had described the script to Mara as safe, and I had no grounds for that word. I had checked that the row counts matched before and after. I had not checked that the rows still held everything they had held. Since then, whenever I move data, I compare a hash of each full row on both sides, and I say out loud what I have not verified. Mara wrote the apology to the support team herself and did not mention me in it, which I noticed and have not forgotten.

I wrote a pattern to strip comments from a configuration file and it was greedy where it should have been cautious: it matched from the first comment marker in the file to the very last line break, and removed everything between. The file went from three hundred lines to two. Mara had it under version control, so nothing was lost but ten minutes. She printed the two surviving lines and pinned them up.
Our reshuffle of client records, where all the tiny comments our helpdesk had jotted for ages vanished: which habit did you adopt afterwards?
Wasn't it a night when a colleague hit the rerun button and all our rehearsal-server appointments appeared in duplicate?
Which check kept breaking solely for me, because I'm an owl, while our early-bird teammate saw nothing amiss at all?
